title: I caught my students using AI to cheat in an exam — here’s what universities must do to stamp this out
excerpt: Without strong standards and smart oversight, artificial intelligence risks eroding the foundations of higher education.
content_html:
• WORLD VIEW
  • 10 August 2026

Without strong standards and smart oversight, artificial intelligence risks eroding the foundations of higher education.

By

  • Roberto Serrano0
  1. Roberto Serrano

    1. Roberto Serrano teaches economics at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, USA.

The rapid spread of generative AI tools has exposed deep vulnerabilities in conventional methods of academic assessment. This challenge came into sharp focus for me when I found evidence of widespread unauthorized use of artificial intelligence in an examination for my course on welfare economics and social-choice theory at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, last semester.

Some students were reluctant to return to the classroom after a campus shooting earlier in the academic year, so I administered the midterm test as a take-home exam for the first time in nearly two decades of teaching the course. Although it was more demanding than previous exams, the average score was 96%, far above the course’s historical range of roughly 65–80%. Suspecting AI-enabled cheating, I held the final test of the course as an in-person, closed-book examination. The average score plummeted to 48.6%. Furthermore, several students either dropped the course or did not sit the final exam.

Why universities need to radically rethink exams in the age of AI

The shocking aspect of this episode was not that cheating seems to have occurred on the take-home exam, but how prevalent it appeared to be. Universities have struggled to respond adequately to this challenge. But they cannot afford to ignore it — the very credibility of learning and assessment is at stake.

Two things require immediate attention: restoring a culture of academic integrity and adapting student learning and assessment methods for the age of AI.

The prevalence of cheating at universities is sustained, at least in part, by the reluctance of academic leaders to confront it decisively. When university leaders fail to defend academic integrity unequivocally, they help to create a culture in which cheating is normalized. My own experience and the countless messages I have received from faculty members at other institutions suggest that administrators often respond to evidence of extensive cheating with hesitation or denial. In some cases, this seems to stem from a desire to protect the institution’s reputation and ‘market value’. Yet, it misunderstands the factors that ultimately give a university its standing: high standards, a strong work ethic and genuine academic excellence.

AI can supercharge inequality — unless the public learns to control it

• 世界观

如果没有强有力的标准和明智的监督，人工智能就有可能侵蚀高等教育的基础。

By

  • 罗伯托·塞拉诺0
  1. 罗伯托·塞拉诺 (Roberto Serrano) 罗伯托·塞拉诺 (Roberto Serrano) 在美国罗德岛州普罗维登斯的布朗大学教授经济学。

生成式人工智能工具的快速传播暴露了传统学术评估方法的深层漏洞。 上学期，当我在罗德岛州普罗维登斯布朗大学的福利经济学和社会选择理论课程考试中发现大量未经授权使用人工智能的证据时，这一挑战成为我关注的焦点。

在学年早些时候发生校园枪击事件后，一些学生不愿意返回课堂，因此我在近二十年的课程教学中首次将期中考试作为带回家的考试进行。 尽管比之前的考试要求更高，但平均分达到了 96%，远高于该课程约 65-80% 的历史范围。 由于怀疑人工智能作弊，我以现场闭卷方式进行了课程的期末考试。 平均分骤降至48.6%。 此外，一些学生要么放弃了课程，要么没有参加期末考试。

为什么大学需要从根本上重新考虑人工智能时代的考试

这一事件的令人震惊的方面并不是带回家的考试中似乎发生了作弊，而是作弊现象似乎非常普遍。 大学一直在努力充分应对这一挑战。 但他们不能忽视这一点——学习和评估的可信度正受到威胁。

有两件事需要立即关注：恢复学术诚信文化，并调整学生的学习和评估方法以适应人工智能时代。

大学中作弊现象的普遍存在，至少部分是由于学术领袖不愿果断地面对作弊行为。 当大学领导者未能明确捍卫学术诚信时，他们就会帮助创造一种使作弊行为常态化的文化。 我自己的经验以及我从其他机构的教员那里收到的无数信息表明，管理人员经常对广泛作弊的证据做出犹豫或否认的反应。 在某些情况下，这似乎源于保护机构声誉和“市场价值”的愿望。 然而，它误解了最终赋予大学地位的因素：高标准、强烈的职业道德和真正的学术卓越。
